{"id": "28:15/q10", "question": "Who was the man from Moses' party?", "turns_on": "Whether the affiliation is ethnic, religious, a particular named person, or an army.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q10/p1", "position": "An Israelite, from Moses' people or followers.", "reasons": "Most reports name an Israelite; some describe him as a religious adherent or believer, others as kin by lineage. Muqatil and al-Suddi say both fighters were unbelievers; Razi cites the next day's rebuke, but prefers a Muslim ally because partisan usually implies shared way."}, {"id": "28:15/q10/p2", "position": "Specifically the Samaritan, who was an Israelite partisan.", "reasons": "Reported by the commentators and repeated by later sources."}, {"id": "28:15/q10/p3", "position": "A member of Moses' army.", "reasons": "Al-Damghani gives the army sense of shiʿa."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q11", "question": "What does 'party' mean here?", "turns_on": "Which aspect of affiliation shiʿa denotes.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q11/p1", "position": "A group affiliated with someone: followers, helpers, companions, or kin.", "reasons": "Ibn Faris gives helpers and factions; a cited poem uses shiʿa for what follows after. Ibn Ashur compares 28:4."}, {"id": "28:15/q11/p2", "position": "An army.", "reasons": "Al-Damghani gives this lexical sense."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q12", "question": "Who was the man called Moses' enemy?", "turns_on": "Whether 'enemy' refers to Egyptian ethnicity and Pharaoh's party, disbelief, or a named royal employee.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q12/p1", "position": "An Egyptian Copt from Pharaoh's people.", "reasons": "This is the prevailing identification. Mujahid adds that Pharaoh was Persian from Istakhr; Zajjaj reports the slain man as Coptic or from Istakhr. The Biblical Exodus account explicitly calls him Egyptian."}, {"id": "28:15/q12/p2", "position": "Specifically Pharaoh's cook or baker, with varying names: Falyathun, Fathun, Fatun, Faq'un, or Qanun.", "reasons": "Reports disagree over his job and name; Sa'id ibn Jubayr calls him the baker, while others call him cook. The spelling varies and is not resolved."}, {"id": "28:15/q12/p3", "position": "Perhaps another Israelite who disbelieved.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports M's speculation; it notes the first opponent is Egyptian in Exodus, while the different wording in verse 19 may concern a distinct second opponent."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q13", "question": "How do the repeated 'this one' demonstratives function?", "turns_on": "Whether the clauses are descriptive or circumstantial, and how present pointing operates in past narration.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q13/p1", "position": "They stage the past, absent men as if present before an observer.", "reasons": "Zajjaj offers both absent-description and eyewitness-style explanations; Abu Ali compares 12:110. Al-Mubarrad cites Jarir for pointing at an absent person; Ibn Ashur says paired demonstratives need not distinguish distance, comparing 4:143 and poetry."}, {"id": "28:15/q13/p2", "position": "Each nominal demonstrative clause describes one of the two men.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas parses subject and predicate. Al-Samin allows description or circumstance, but calls the latter remote because the state is not changing. Al-Alusi says demonstratives link the descriptions back to the men."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q14", "question": "What does the Israelite's appeal mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q14/p1", "position": "He asked Moses to rescue or support him against his opponent.", "reasons": "The verb derives from ghawth, help. Baydawi and Alusi explain ala through the sense of support or victory; Alusi cites the next day's appeal. Ibn Ashur infers the Israelite was overpowered."}, {"id": "28:15/q14/p2", "position": "The expression also exposes a duty to help the oppressed.", "reasons": "Qurtubi calls this a duty in every revealed law; Ibn Ashur says coerced work was unjust."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q15", "question": "How is the appeal verb read?", "turns_on": "Whether the transmitted assistance form is a valid reading and whether its contextual fit warrants preference.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q15/p1", "position": "The common reading is fastaghāthahu, 'he sought rescue'.", "reasons": "Al-Samin derives it from ghawth; Abu Hayyan calls it the majority reading."}, {"id": "28:15/q15/p2", "position": "An assistance reading, istaʿānahu, replaces rescue with asking aid.", "reasons": "Attributed to Sibawayh, Ibn Miqsam and al-Zafarani. Ibn Jabbarah prefers it for context; Ibn Atiyya calls it a corruption or scribal error, challenged by Abu Hayyan and al-Samin on transmitted evidence. Al-Alusi questions Ibn Atiyya's attribution to al-Akhfash."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q16", "question": "What is omitted in 'the one from his party'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q16/p1", "position": "The relative clauses omit their subjects: 'the one who is from his party' and 'the one who is from his enemy'.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi makes the ellipsis explicit."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q17", "question": "What does wakz mean and where does it land?", "turns_on": "Whether the word denotes a fist blow or fingertip push and where synonymous or near-synonymous blows are placed.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q17/p1", "position": "A thrust, push, or strike with the hand, often a closed fist or gathered palm.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Tabari and many others specify gathered fingers; some put the blow at the chest, heart, torso, jaw or across the body. Lexicographers compare lakz, nakz, nahz and lahz; Ru'ba's and other cited poetry illustrate the word and related verbs. Abu Zayd's and Aisha's reports illustrate painful pushing."}, {"id": "28:15/q17/p2", "position": "More narrowly, a push with the fingertips.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda and al-Farra define it this way; Razi repeats it. Al-Samin says other authorities reverse the wakz/lakz distinction."}, {"id": "28:15/q17/p3", "position": "The exact contrast with lakz varies: wakz at chest, heart or torso; lakz at back, jaw or palate.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Razi give chest versus back; Ibn Atiyya gives torso versus jaw. Qurtubi gives heart versus jaw and Abu Ubayda's chest sense; al-Samin records reversed assignments."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q18", "question": "What did Moses strike him with?", "turns_on": "Whether the report follows Mujahid's hand account or Qatada's staff account; the lexical suitability of wakz is contested.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q18/p1", "position": "With his hand, palm or clenched fist.", "reasons": "Many sources attribute this to Mujahid; Moses' exceptional strength made one blow fatal. Variants describe a whole hand, gathered fist, or fist shape counted as seventy-three or eighty-three."}, {"id": "28:15/q18/p2", "position": "With a staff or stick.", "reasons": "Qatada is the recurrent authority. Al-Mufaddal objects that wakz is not used of a staff; Al-Alusi notes Moses' famous staff came later from Shuayb and suggests this would have been another staff."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q19", "question": "What alternative words are read for wakz?", "turns_on": "Which transmitted consonant is read and whether the verbs differ materially.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q19/p1", "position": "The ordinary text has fawakazahu.", "reasons": "Most lexical discussions gloss this form as a push or blow."}, {"id": "28:15/q19/p2", "position": "Ibn Masud or Abdullah reads falakazahu.", "reasons": "The reports generally treat lakz as close in meaning to wakz, though some distinguish jaw/back from torso/chest."}, {"id": "28:15/q19/p3", "position": "Abdullah or Ibn Masud also has fanakazahu.", "reasons": "Al-Farra says wakz, nakz and wahz share a meaning; other sources say nakz is pushing or striking, with a poem showing a snake's jab."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q20", "question": "What does 'he finished him' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q20/p1", "position": "The man died: Moses' blow killed or finished him.", "reasons": "Qaḍā ʿalayhi also means finishing an affair; Jarir and al-Ashja are cited for the death idiom. Al-Mubarrad says his appointed time arrived; Baydawi compares 15:66. Bursevi's Mufradat explanation links death with completing one's allotted term."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q21", "question": "Who is the subject of 'finished him'?", "turns_on": "Which agent is supplied to the verb: Moses, God, or the fatal blow/death.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q21/p1", "position": "Moses is the apparent subject.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi calls this the obvious syntax. Ibn Ashur reports the view but says it is not evident."}, {"id": "28:15/q21/p2", "position": "God is the subject, decreeing the Copt's death.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites 34:14 for God as the one who decrees death; Abu Hayyan and Alusi list it."}, {"id": "28:15/q21/p3", "position": "The implied blow or death itself is the subject.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin list the blow; Ibn Ashur describes an omitted agent, death, in the fixed idiom."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q22", "question": "Did Moses intend to kill the man?", "turns_on": "Whether a forceful blow from Moses could reasonably be expected to kill, and whether he could have used a gentler means.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q22/p1", "position": "No; he intended a push or intervention and the blow unexpectedly caused death.", "reasons": "Qatada, Ibn Ishaq and others say this explicitly. His exceptional strength made one blow fatal; Qurtubi's Ka'b report gives Moses' age as twelve. Ibn Ashur says it struck a vital spot, while Tabatabai points to the absence of the explicit killing verb."}, {"id": "28:15/q22/p2", "position": "The fatal outcome could have been foreseeable given Moses' strength; accident alone does not settle blame.", "reasons": "Razi rejects the inference of accidental death, saying a strong man's blow could certainly kill a weak man. He says Moses could have freed the Israelite another way even if the death was accidental."}]}

'this is Satan's work'?", "turns_on": "What 'this' points to and whether Satan's influence concerns anger, the fight, the victim, or partisan judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q23/p1", "position": "Satan incited Moses' anger or harsh blow, leading to the death.", "reasons": "Moses had not been commanded to kill. Qushayri distinguishes Satan's prompting of severity from attributing the death itself to Satan. Al-Alusi prefers prompting or embellishment because it fits the ensuing description. Ibn Ashur allows 'this' to point to blow, death, or anger."}, {"id": "28:15/q23/p2", "position": "'This' is the fight or hostility between the men, which Satan stirred.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says min may mean kind or origin; the fight brought Moses into peril. Al-Rida's report says Moses killed by God's command, while Satan's work denotes the men's fight."}, {"id": "28:15/q23/p3", "position": "'This' is the slain man's conduct, which was Satanic and made him deserve death.", "reasons": "Al-Murtada and Razi transmit this reading; Razi also reports taking the man himself as belonging to Satan's faction."}, {"id": "28:15/q23/p4", "position": "The deed was of the same kind as Satan's work, without asserting direct prompting.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this alternative but prefers the direct prompting explanation."}, {"id": "28:15/q23/p5", "position": "The error lay in tribal favoritism: Moses helped his kin without judging the dispute and killed an innocent man.", "reasons": "Asad reads verses 16–17 this way and cites Prophetic condemnation of fighting for one's group or helping it unjustly."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q24", "question": "How should Moses' deed and remorse be judged?", "turns_on": "Whether the man could lawfully be killed, Moses' intent and prophetic status, and whether remorse marks sin, a lesser choice, or nonculpable error.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q24/p1", "position": "He sinned by killing before permission or while under a protected status, and repented.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan says fighting unbelievers was barred then; Ibn Jurayj says a prophet may kill only by command. Kashshaf calls it a sin requiring repentance. Nasafi and Baydawi add that protected residence made an attack unlawful."}, {"id": "28:15/q24/p2", "position": "His intervention was good defense of an oppressed person; the killing was accidental, not a culpable sin.", "reasons": "Tabrisi says defensive pain is good; Qushayri invokes divine decree to explain why one blow killed. Tabatabai calls the misguidance a harmful practical error, comparing Adam; Kuran Yolu says a slap rarely kills and Moses' guilt reflects the outcome."}, {"id": "28:15/q24/p3", "position": "The killing may have been permitted, but delaying it or choosing a gentler rescue was preferable.", "reasons": "Al-Murtada and Razi describe forfeiting the reward of a recommended course; Razi says Moses could seek forgiveness for the lesser choice even if killing was lawful or accidental. Biqai says lack of specific command, not impermissibility, caused regret."}, {"id": "28:15/q24/p4", "position": "A killing by God's command is compatible with calling the men's fight Satanic.", "reasons": "Al-Rida's report separates the commanded killing from Satan's instigation of the quarrel."}, {"id": "28:15/q24/p5", "position": "The verse raises a challenge about prophetic protection from sin.", "reasons": "Critics argue that regret is puzzling whether the Copt deserved death or not, and ask why accidental death requires forgiveness. Razi answers that legal status varies by dispensation, a gentler course was possible, and Moses' prophethood at that moment is not established. Shawkani distinguishes major and minor sin; Kuran Yolu places the act before prophecy."}, {"id": "28:15/q24/p6", "position": "He killed in wrongful tribal partisanship.", "reasons": "Asad says verses 16–17 show the Israelite at fault; prophetic reports condemn aiding one's people in an unjust cause."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q25", "question": "Who does 'he' refer to, and what does the Satan description say?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q25/p1", "position": "The pronoun is Satan, the clear enemy and misleader of Adam's descendants.", "reasons": "Tabari says Satan beautifies ugly acts; Ibn Ashur says the omitted object of enmity is Adam and his offspring. Samarai distinguishes Satan's abiding and active misleading from God's abiding and renewed guidance."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q26", "question": "How are 'enemy, misleader, manifest' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether mubīn specifies Satan's enmity, his misguidance, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q26/p1", "position": "They can be successive predicates or adjectives; mubīn describes manifest enmity.", "reasons": "Nahhas lists both parses; Qurtubi calls the enemy description a second predicate. Al-Alusi treats mubīn as a second adjective of enemy and derives it from intransitive abāna."}, {"id": "28:15/q26/p2", "position": "Mubīn modifies 'misleader' or both 'enemy' and 'misleader'.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur takes it with misleading; Al-Alusi reports a shared-adjective or implicit-wording analysis."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q27", "question": "What theological implication is drawn from Satan's role?", "turns_on": "Whether divine causation is compatible with calling the event Satan's work.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q27/p1", "position": "The killing and misguidance are not created by God; Satan's censure as misleader excludes God's causing misguidance.", "reasons": "Jishumi argues against determinists, saying attribution and blame would be incoherent if God created the deed or misleading. Razi reports the Mu'tazilite argument with parallels from Joseph, Moses' companion, and Adam's parents."}, {"id": "28:15/q27/p2", "position": "God creates causes when He wills an outcome, including the one fatal blow.", "reasons": "Qushayri says many blows may fail to kill, while this one fulfilled the decreed death."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q28", "question": "How does this incident connect to the wider Moses narrative?", "turns_on": "How the event functions as the narrative hinge from maturation in Egypt to accusation and migration.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q28/p1", "position": "The killing begins the chain leading to Moses' departure for Midian and later prophetic calling.", "reasons": "Biqai sees the transition from preparation to migration; Ibn Kathir says it fulfilled the divine decree; Tabatabai situates the episode after maturity. Ibn Ashur says the empty hour explains lack of witnesses and prepares for the accusation in verse 19."}, {"id": "28:15/q28/p2", "position": "Moses' palace lay outside or at the edge of the city, illuminating the later messenger from its far side.", "reasons": "Bursevi and Tabatabai link the entry route to 28:20."}, {"id": "28:15/q28/p3", "position": "The next day's appeal and accusation show how the killing became known.", "reasons": "Sa'id ibn Jubayr's report says another opponent recognized Moses as yesterday's killer, leading to flight; Ibn Ashur links the accusation to 28:19."}, {"id": "28:15/q28/p4", "position": "Moses' present act followed his maturation and developing Israelite identity.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says his standing curtailed Egyptian oppression. Ibn Ashur suggests his mother disclosed his origins, explaining solidarity with Israelites; Razi says wisdom and knowledge preceded this killing."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q29", "question": "What inward reading is given to the city, combat, and killing?", "turns_on": "Whether the spiritual killing signifies overcoming passion or an excessive countermeasure.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q29/p1", "position": "The city is the body; quiet psychic powers let the heart aid intellect against passion.", "reasons": "Qashani maps the two men to intellect and passion, and Moses' intervention to practical wisdom and angelic aid overcoming satanic fancy."}, {"id": "28:15/q29/p2", "position": "The killing warns against treating one extreme vice with its opposite rather than with merciful justice.", "reasons": "Qashani lists greed checked by lethargy, miserliness by extravagance, and wastefulness by stinginess."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q30", "question": "What surrounding report details explain Moses' situation and reaction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q30/p1", "position": "Moses' anger at the Copt's assault led to the fatal blow, witnessed only by God and the Israelite.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas gives this detail; Ibn Ashur cites Exodus saying Moses looked around and buried the man in sand."}, {"id": "28:15/q30/p2", "position": "Moses was called Pharaoh's son.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports this as one account of his status."}, {"id": "28:15/q30/p3", "position": "Wahb reports God pardoned Moses because the slain man had never acknowledged God as creator or provider.", "reasons": "The report says even one acknowledgment would have brought punishment."}]}

{"id": "28:15/q32", "question": "How does fāʾ express the sequence from blow to death?", "turns_on": "Whether fāʾ conveys causal succession or a looser discourse order.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q32/p1", "position": "Fāʾ marks causal result: the blow caused death.", "reasons": "Burhan says fāʾ can combine coordination and causation; Itqan compares Adam receiving words and repenting. {"id": "28:15/q35", "question": "What is reported about the revelation of Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q35/p1", "position": "All of al-Qaṣaṣ is Meccan.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports Hasan, Ata and Ikrima for this view."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q36", "question": "What reading authority is ascribed to Nāfiʿ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q36/p1", "position": "His Medinan reading was selected by agreement among leading readers and became the community's authoritative practice.", "reasons": "Nāfiʿ describes choosing readings agreed by two of five. An unnamed report places it already by 100 AH; a disciple says his reading saved assembling one independently. His final admonition echoes 8:1."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q37", "question": "What pronunciation of ṣād and neighboring consonants does Sībawayh describe?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q37/p1", "position": "Before dhāl, unvowelled ṣād approaches or becomes zāy, while moving ṣād is best kept clear.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says emphatic ṣād can approximate the nearest voiced zāy but full conversion is also spoken; moving ṣād cannot be replaced. Sīn in the same place shifts to zāy, and shīn or jīm may approximate it, with examples."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q38", "question": "How are certain defective nouns and vocatives formed?", "turns_on": "The distinct morphological analogies for dual formation and vocative shortening.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q38/p1", "position": "Defective four-letter nouns form duals and plurals with yāʾ, whether their alif replaces a root or is augmentative.", "reasons": "Sībawayh explains both by analogy with corresponding verbs, including wāw-root forms and examples ḥublā and maʿzā."}, {"id": "28:15/q38/p2", "position": "Quadriliteral-like wāw and yāʾ behave as added, radical-like letters and remain under vocative shortening.", "reasons": "Sībawayh cites qanūr and habīj, their capacity for further augmentations, and avoidance of deleting two letters; Manṣūr may shorten to Manṣ."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q39", "question": "How do commands, supplications and topicalization affect case and fāʾ?", "turns_on": "Whether preposed nouns are command objects, topics, or resumptions of implied prior discourse.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q39/p1", "position": "An object before a command is normally accusative under an overt or implied verb.", "reasons": "Sībawayh covers direct and prepositional objects, amā clauses, and third-person commands; commands require a verb more strongly than interrogatives. A nominative topic is possible with an understood context, but 'Zayd fa-ḍribhu' cannot be an ordinary subject; its object pronoun must remain."}, {"id": "28:15/q39/p2", "position": "A relative or generalized topic with conditional force can take fāʾ in its predicate.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives all-man and relative-clause examples and cites 2:274. He distinguishes this from a simple Zayd topic."}, {"id": "28:15/q39/p3", "position": "Revelatory law verses begin with raised nouns under an implied context, though accusative readings exist.", "reasons": "Sībawayh analyzes 24:2, 5:38 and 4:16 through an antecedent topic about ordinances and notes some readers' accusative forms."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q40", "question": "What rhetorical principles about simile, metaphor and predication are cited?", "turns_on": "What part of rhetorical meaning comes from transfer, predication, qualification, or discourse knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q40/p1", "position": "Simile asserts likeness, while metaphor transfers a term and parable constructs a comparison.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani distinguishes sensory likeness and intellectual tamthil, insists an explicit simile is literal, and says context settles a borrowed noun such as 'lion' or figurative verbs."}, {"id": "28:15/q40/p2", "position": "Metaphor's force exceeds merely stating a strong resemblance.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani rejects explanations by resemblance alone or by wording-versus-meaning; the pearl, narcissus, rose and hail images work by asserting intensity delightfully."}, {"id": "28:15/q40/p3", "position": "Unfavorable images in praise must be cushioned by favorable context.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani analyzes night, wormwood and honey, the Mutanabbi's beauty and ugliness, and criticizes Abu Tammam's unguarded low-status names."}, {"id": "28:15/q40/p4", "position": "One may pair literal and figurative images only when the two referents truly differ in status.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani rejects the two-rains example as both metaphorical, accepts the two-lions example, and explains the abstract benefit in al-Farazdaq's rain comparison."}, {"id": "28:15/q40/p5", "position": "A full proposition requires predication of one term of another, with qualifiers depending on that base.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani identifies musnad and musnad ilayh and analyzes 'Zayd struck' and al-Farazdaq's negation; grammatical restrictions and intention build the meaning."}, {"id": "28:15/q40/p6", "position": "Complements and definiteness shape an act's and predicate's sense.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani says a verbal noun's object changes the type of action; definite derived predicates express characteristic capacity, while alladhī identifies a referent by information already known."}]}
{"id": "28:15/q41", "question": "How does the Qur'an's arrangement and style establish its distinctiveness?", "turns_on": "Whether distinctive form, mixed arrangement, or the unanswered challenge is the cited proof.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q41/p1", "position": "Its distinctive speech exceeds familiar poetry, rhymed prose, sermons, letters and ordinary speech.", "reasons": "Al-Rummani compares its departure from convention to a handwoven cloth exceeding the finest machine work and to miracles of the sea and staff; changing rhyme endings does not reproduce authorship."}, {"id": "28:15/q41/p2", "position": "Mixing stories, warnings and rulings within a sura gives a listener access to proofs across subjects.", "reasons": "Al-Khattabi reports the contrary criticism that segregating topics would improve organization, then argues for the broad benefit of their combination."}, {"id": "28:15/q41/p3", "position": "The prolonged challenge and opponents' failure to answer prove the Qur'an could not be fabricated.", "reasons": "Al-Baqillani notes charges of fabrication and borrowed tales; he argues that hostile opponents faced severe losses yet never produced an easy verbal counter in their own language."}]}
